To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we were able to produce cartilaginous tissue constructs that express endostatin using nonviral gene delivery and that these engineered constructs can be cultured for several weeks without compromising chondrogenesis.

the nonviral expression of endostatin in collagen scaffolds is tunable with the following variables: scaffold material, method, and load of nonviral transgene incorporation, culture medium, oxygen tension, and cell type.

endostatin was overexpressed in chondrocytic and mesenchymale stem cell (MSC)-seeded collagen scaffolds using nonviral vector transfection, that endostatin overexpression did not inhibit chondrogenesis, and that the amount of endostation produced was tunable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new class of biomaterials for tissue engineering.
the development of an engineered cartilaginous tissue with the potential to repair articular cartilage defects.
developing a novel tissue-engineered cartilage construct that inhibits angiogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the nonviral transduction of chondroprogenitor cells to overexpress the anti-angiogenic factor endostatin in a scaffold environment was successful, with endostatin expression tunable by external factors.
the nonviral endostatin expression system can be used to engineer endostain-expressing cartilage constructs.

the nonviral endostatin gene transfer method described in the present study can be used to engineer endostain-expressing cartilage constructs that can potentially be used to modulate angiogenesis during the tissue-engineering process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a method for engineering endostatin-exposing cartilaginous tissue constructs, which can be used to study the effect of endostatin on cartilage regeneration.
the nonviral endostatin vector was effective for transfecting chondrocytic cells, and the transfection was tunable to the extent that it was possible to control the amount of endostain produced.

we were able to engineer a collagen scaffold-based cartilagous construct that overexpresses endostatin using a nonviral transfectant, without affecting the viability of the cells and the chondrogenesis of the construct.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to engineer endostating producing cartilage-like constructs using nonviral vector technology.
it is feasible to use nonviral vectors to engineer cartilaginous tissue overexpressing endostatin.
endostatin expression can be sustained for at least 1 week in the collagen scaffold constructs.
